lines: Take a sorted sequence, cut it at some point nobody tells you, and swap the two pieces around.
Your gut says that breaks the search. It doesn't. It only breaks the lazy version of the search.
Look at the middle value here, and compare it with where the range starts.
Which side of that middle is still climbing in order, and which side would you actually search next?
answer: The side that starts lower than its own middle is the one still in order.
Once you know the target isn't sitting inside that orderly side's own range, you throw the whole thing away and search the other half instead.

lines: One comparison tells you which half still climbs in order. One more tells you whether what you want could even be hiding in it.
Get both answers, and you already know which half to throw away.
The point where the order actually broke is itself just another target to narrow in on.
Ask the same halving question, aimed at a different thing: has this stopped climbing yet?
Now make the start, the middle and the end of the range all read the same value.
Suddenly neither comparison tells you anything, because a run of repeats looks identical no matter which side it sits on.
Build a long run of one repeated value with a single different value buried near the end, and watching this loop crawl toward it one step at a time is the whole lesson.
Picture a grid where every row climbs left to right, and every column climbs top to bottom, but there's no single line you could draw through the whole thing in sorted order.
Does the same halving trick from a moment ago still apply here?
answer: No, and for a specific reason: there's no one question whose answer flips exactly once across the whole grid.
Two separate orders are running at once, and halving needs exactly one.

lines: Start from the corner where one direction only grows and the other only shrinks.
Every single comparison throws an entire row or an entire column away for good — never just one cell.
Add one more rule: every row has to end lower than the next row begins.
Do that, and reading the whole grid one row after another becomes a single climbing line again, which means the halving trick is back, in full.
Take that same rule away, even though every row and column still climbs on its own, and the line breaks, and halving stops working.
Three different grids, three different reasons a question like "which half do I keep" has a different answer each time.
Up to now, every search in this chapter has leaned on an order that was already there to find. The next question starts with no order at all.
